name: cycle
description: A depends on B depends on A, via parent_task_id. Should not happen, and it will. HierarchyFixture permits this on purpose -- it does not enforce acyclicity -- so this graph loads; what the propagation code does with it is the decision this fixture records.

nodes.label: Leaf under the cycle -- without this, leaf_ids() is empty and no leaf-starting walk ever enters the loop

notes: Decision: detect the cycle and refuse (raise) -- see README.md's Design decisions, "Cycle: detect and refuse, not a depth limit" for the full rationale. HierarchyFixture deliberately does not forbid a cycle: not realistic in the sense that any real data source would produce one today (neither Chain's traversal API nor the eval's own validator ever lets one through), but it is realistic in the sense that the type permits constructing it, so defensive code walking an arbitrary HierarchyFixture must handle it regardless. A naive walk-the-parent-chain implementation loops forever here -- that's the whole point of this fixture. Separate fact, not a justification for the above: Chain's own ancestorIds traversal does not treat a cycle as an error either -- it silently stops and returns the chain collected so far with a normal 200, so Mind cannot rely on Chain's API to ever surface one (relevant to #474's Chain adapter, not to this fixture's decision). task_in_cycle exists only so leaf_ids() is non-empty and a leaf-starting walk actually reaches the cycle.
